title: Rambour: religious honor for God alone; civil honor of the heavenly city for Saints and angels
source_text: XIII. Sic mentem suam ea de re explicat Abrahamus Ramburtius. Sciendum est, inquit, duplicem esse honorem. Est religiosus soli Deo debitus: est civilis creaturis adhibitus. Civilis rursus impenditur, vel respectu civitatis mundanae, qui complectitur omnia officia reverentiae, amoris, timoris, qui hominibus debetur etiamsi sint a fide alieni. Sic principes, parentes, senes, sapientes, concives honoramus. Vel civilis dicitur ratione civitatis supernae, quo honore domesticos fidei prosequimur: atque huc pertinet mutua illa qua nos invicem complectimur, Rom. 12. 10. & professio officiosae opinionis quam concipimus de fratribus nostris, Philip. 2. 3. & sollicitudo qua invicem afficiuntur membra. Deinde observantia & reverentia, juxta varias conditiones, excellentiae dotes, atque etiam gloriam eorum, qui civitatem illam supernam constituunt. Atque hoc sensu honoramus Sanctos & Angelos, charitate, ut loquitur Augustinus, non servitute, cultu dilectionis & societatis, quo in hac vita coluntur Sancti Dei, ut supra dictum est. Laudamus eos debito modo, amamus, imitamur quantum possumus, eorundem virtutes praedicamus, ut zelus noster augeatur & incalescat. In Thesauro thesium Sedanensium, tom. 2. Thesibus de cultu Religioso & Idololatrico, th. 16.
pass_a_gloss: Abraham Rambour explains his mind on this matter thus. It is to be known, he says, that honor is twofold. There is a religious honor owed to God alone, and a civil honor applied to creatures. Civil honor is again paid either with respect to the worldly city, which embraces all the offices of reverence, love, and fear owed to men even if they are strangers to the faith: thus we honor princes, parents, the aged, the wise, and fellow citizens. Or it is called civil by reason of the heavenly city, by which honor we attend the household of faith: and hither belongs that mutual embrace by which we embrace one another, Romans 12. 10, the dutiful profession of the opinion we form of our brothers, Philippians 2. 3, and the care by which the members are affected toward one another. Then observance and reverence, according to various conditions, gifts of excellence, and also the glory of those who constitute that heavenly city. And in this sense we honor Saints and angels, with charity, as Augustine says, not with servitude, with a cult of love and society, by which the Saints of God are cultivated in this life, as was said above. We praise them in the due way, we love them, we imitate them as far as we can, we proclaim their virtues, so that our zeal may be increased and grow warm. In the Treasury of the Sedan theses, volume 2, theses on religious cult and idolatry, thesis 16.
pass_b_english: Rambour divides honor into religious honor owed to God alone and civil honor given to creatures.
Civil honor of the earthly city covers reverence, love, and fear even toward people outside the faith.
Civil honor of the heavenly city is how the household of faith is treated, including mutual esteem in Romans 12 and Philippians 2.
Saints and angels receive that second civil honor: charity and fellowship, not servitude, by praise, love, imitation, and the stirring of zeal.

choices.why: This is the Reformed sense of civil honor for Saints, distinct from worldly courtesy.
